questions.title: GATE CE 2017 Set 1 | CE Q1
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.question: The matrix \(\mathbf{P}\) is the inverse of a matrix \(\mathbf{Q}\). If \(\mathbf{I}\) denotes the identity matrix, which one of the following options is correct?
questions.explanation:
Engineering Mathematics | Linear Algebra / Matrices

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension
  • Given Data: Matrix \(\mathbf{P}\) is the inverse of matrix \(\mathbf{Q}\); \(\mathbf{I}\) denotes the identity matrix.
  • Aim: Identify the correct relationship between \(\mathbf{P}\), \(\mathbf{Q}\), and \(\mathbf{I}\).

3. Core Concepts:

  • Definition of Matrix Inverse: For a square matrix \(\mathbf{Q}\), if inverse \(\mathbf{P}\) exists, then \(\mathbf{Q} imes \mathbf{P}\) yields the identity matrix \(\mathbf{I}\).
  • Commutativity of Inverses: Although matrix multiplication is generally not commutative, a matrix and its inverse do commute:
    \[\mathbf{P} = \mathbf{Q}^{-1} \iff \mathbf{PQ} = \mathbf{QP} = \mathbf{I} \]

4. Solution Method:

From \(\mathbf{P} = \mathbf{Q}^{-1}\), multiply both sides by \(\mathbf{Q}\) on the right and on the left to verify both products equal \(\mathbf{I}\).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Option (A): \(\mathbf{PQ} = \mathbf{I}\) but \(\mathbf{QP} eq \mathbf{I}\) — Incorrect (they must commute).
  2. Option (B): \(\mathbf{QP} = \mathbf{I}\) but \(\mathbf{PQ} eq \mathbf{I}\) — Incorrect.
  3. Option (C): \(\mathbf{PQ} = \mathbf{I}\) and \(\mathbf{QP} = \mathbf{I}\) — Correct.
  4. Option (D): \(\mathbf{PQ} - \mathbf{QP} = \mathbf{I} \implies \mathbf{I} - \mathbf{I} = \mathbf{0} eq \mathbf{I}\) — Incorrect.

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: \(\mathbf{PQ} = \mathbf{I}\) and \(\mathbf{QP} = \mathbf{I}\)  |  Correct option: (C)

3. Core Concepts:

  • Gaussian (Normal) Distribution: Models continuous data clustering around a central mean.

    Defined by two parameters: mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Exponential parameters = 1 (\(\lambda\)).
  2. Gaussian parameters = 2 (\(\mu,\ \sigma\)).

questions.question: Let \(x\) be a continuous variable defined over the interval \((-\infty, \infty)\), and \(f(x) = e^{-x} - e^{-x}\). The integral \(g(x) = \displaystyle \int f(x) \, dx\) is equal to
questions.explanation:
Engineering Mathematics | Calculus / Integrals

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data: \(x \in (-\infty,\infty)\); function \(f(x) = e^{-x - e^{-x}}\)
    Correction Note: OCR may parse the function as \(e^{-x} - e^{-x}\) (which equals 0). The correct form, visible in the screenshot, is the nested exponent \(f(x) = e^{-x-e^{-x}}\).
  • Aim: Evaluate \(g(x) = \int f(x)\, dx\).

3. Core Concepts:

  • Integration by Substitution: Change variables to simplify the integrand.
  • Exponent Rule: \(e^{A+B} = e^A \cdot e^B \implies e^{-x-e^{-x}} = e^{-x} \cdot e^{-e^{-x}}\)
  • Standard Result: \( \displaystyle \int e^u\, du = e^u + C\)

4. Solution Method:

Rewrite the integral as \( \displaystyle \int e^{-x} \cdot e^{-e^{-x}}\, dx\), then use the substitution \(u = e^{-x}\).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Let \(u = e^{-x}\).
  2. Differentiate: \(\dfrac{du}{dx} = -e^{-x} \implies du = -e^{-x}\, dx \implies -du = e^{-x}\, dx\).
  3. Substitute:
    \[\int e^{-x} \cdot e^{-e^{-x}}\, dx = \int e^{-u}(-du) = -\int e^{-u}\, du \]
  4. Evaluate:
    \[-\int e^{-u}\, du = e^{-u} + C \]
  5. Substitute back \(u = e^{-x}\):
    \[g(x) = e^{-e^{-x}} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: \(e^{-e^{-x}}\)  |  Correct option: (B)

questions.title: GATE CE 2017 Set 1 | CE Q4

questions.question: An elastic bar of length \(L\), uniform cross sectional area \(A\), coefficient of thermal expansion \(\alpha\), and Young's modulus \(E\) is fixed at the two ends. The temperature of the bar is increased by \(T\), resulting in an axial stress \(\sigma\). Keeping all other parameters unchanged, if the length of the bar is doubled, the axial stress would be
questions.explanation:
Solid Mechanics | Strength of Materials / Thermal Stresses

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension
  • Given Data:
    • Bar: Length \(L\), area \(A\), thermal expansion coefficient \(\alpha\), Young's modulus \(E\)
    • Both ends strictly fixed; temperature increase \(T\)
    • Initial axial stress \(= \sigma\)
    • New condition: length becomes \(2L\); all other parameters unchanged
  • Aim: Determine the new axial stress.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Free Thermal Expansion: If free to expand, \(\Delta L = L\alpha T\).
  • Restrained Strain: With fixed ends, actual expansion is zero. The restrained mechanical strain equals the prevented thermal strain:
    \[\varepsilon = \dfrac{\Delta L}{L} = \dfrac{L\alpha T}{L} = \alpha T \]
  • Thermal Stress (Hooke's Law): \(\sigma = E\varepsilon = E\alpha T\)

4. Solution Method:

Express the initial axial stress: \(\sigma = E\alpha T\). Observe that this expression is completely independent of \(L\). Doubling \(L\) leaves \(\sigma\) unchanged.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Prevented free expansion: \(\Delta L = L\alpha T\).
  2. Compressive strain: \(\varepsilon = \dfrac{L\alpha T}{L} = \alpha T\).
  3. New thermal stress: \(\sigma_{new} = E \cdot \alpha T = \sigma\).
  4. Length \(L\) cancels algebraically — the stress is unchanged.

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: \(\sigma\)  |  Correct option: (A)

questions.explanation:
Solid Mechanics | Structural Analysis / Bending and Shear in Beams

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data: A simply supported beam subjected to a Uniformly Distributed Load (UDL).
  • Aim: Identify the definitively true statements among the options relating Shear Force (SF), Bending Moment (BM), and Curvature.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Euler-Bernoulli Beam Theory: Curvature \(\kappa = M/(EI)\) — proportional to BM; zero where BM is zero.
  • Differential Relations:
    \[V = \dfrac{dM}{dx}, \qquad w = -\dfrac{dV}{dx} \]
  • Extrema Condition: BM is maximum/minimum where its derivative (SF) is zero.

4. Solution Method:

For a simply supported beam of length \(L\) under UDL \(w\):

  • Reactions: \(R_A = R_B = wL/2\)
  • \(V(x) = wL/2 - wx\) — max/min at ends (\(x=0, L\))
  • \(M(x) = \dfrac{wLx}{2} - \dfrac{wx^2}{2}\) — max at \(x = L/2\), zero at ends
  • \(\kappa(x) = M(x)/(EI)\) — zero at ends, max at midspan

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Statement A: Max/min SF at supports (\(x=0,L\)). At supports, \(M=0 \implies \kappa=0\). True ✓
  2. Statement B: By \(dM/dx = V\), BM is maximum where \(V=0\) (at \(x=L/2\)). True ✓
  3. Statement C: Curvature is zero at \(x=0,L\), but max BM is at midspan (where curvature is maximum, not zero). False ✗
  4. Statement D: Max BM is at midspan; max SF is at supports — different sections. False ✗

Note: GATE officially accepted both A and B as correct for this beam configuration.

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: Statements A and B  |  Correct option: (A) or (B) (as per official GATE key)

questions.subject: Structural Analysis & Mechanics
questions.question:
The figure shows a two-hinged parabolic arch of span \(L\) subjected to a uniformly distributed load of intensity \(q\) per unit length.

The maximum bending moment in the arch is equal to
questions.explanation:
Structural Analysis | Arches / Two-Hinged Parabolic Arch

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Structure: Two-hinged parabolic arch
    • Span \(= L\), rise \(= h\)
    • Loading: UDL \(q\) per unit length over the entire span
  • Aim: Find the maximum bending moment in the arch.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Arch geometry: \(y = \dfrac{4hx(L-x)}{L^2}\)
  • Net bending moment at section \(x\): \(M_x = M_{beam} - H \cdot y\)
  • Horizontal thrust for full-span UDL: \(H = \dfrac{qL^2}{8h}\)

4. Solution Method:

Compute \(M_{beam}\) and \(H \cdot y\) at a generic section \(x\), then subtract.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Simply supported beam moment:
    \[M_{beam} = \dfrac{qLx}{2} - \dfrac{qx^2}{2} = \dfrac{q}{2}x(L-x) \]
  2. Moment from horizontal thrust:
    \[H \cdot y = \dfrac{qL^2}{8h} \cdot \dfrac{4hx(L-x)}{L^2} = \dfrac{q}{2}x(L-x) \]
  3. Net bending moment:
    \[M_x = \dfrac{q}{2}x(L-x) - \dfrac{q}{2}x(L-x) = 0 \]

The bending moment is zero at every section. The arch acts as a funicular structure for a uniform load, transmitting forces purely through axial compression.

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: Zero  |  Correct option: (C)

questions.question: A strip footing is resting on the ground surface of a pure clay bed having an undrained cohesion \(c_u\). The ultimate bearing capacity of the footing is equal to
questions.explanation:

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Recall / Application
  • Given Data:
    • Footing type: Strip footing on the ground surface (\(D_f = 0\))
    • Soil: Pure clay (\(\phi = 0^\circ\)), undrained cohesion \(= c_u\)
  • Aim: Calculate the ultimate bearing capacity (\(q_u\)).

3. Core Concepts:

  • Terzaghi's General Bearing Capacity Equation:
    \[q_u = c N_c + q N_q + 0.5\,\gamma B N_\gamma \]
  • Prandtl's Exact Plasticity Solution for strip footing on purely cohesive soil:
    \[N_c = \pi + 2 \approx 5.14 \]
  • Surface footing: \(D_f = 0 \implies q = \gamma D_f = 0\)
  • Pure clay (\(\phi = 0^\circ\)): \(N_\gamma = 0\), \(N_q = 1\)

4. Solution Method:

The second and third terms vanish. The equation reduces to \(q_u = c_u N_c\). The presence of \(\pi\) in the answer options indicates use of Prandtl's exact solution where \(N_c = \pi + 2\).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. \(q_u = c_u N_c + 0 + 0 = c_u N_c\)
  2. \(N_c = (\pi + 2)\) (Prandtl's exact plasticity solution)
  3. \(q_u = (\pi + 2)\,c_u\)

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: \((\pi + 2)c_u\)  |  Correct option: (D)

questions.question: A uniformly distributed line load of 500 kN/m is acting on the ground surface. Based on Boussinesq's theory, the ratio of vertical stress at a depth 2 m to that at 4 m, right below the line of loading, is
questions.explanation:
Geotechnical Engineering | Soil Mechanics / Stress Distribution in Soils

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Line load: \(q = 500\text{ kN/m}\)
    • Depth 1: \(z_1 = 2\text{ m}\), Depth 2: \(z_2 = 4\text{ m}\)
  • Aim: Find the ratio of vertical stress at \(z_1\) to that at \(z_2\) directly below the line load (\(x = 0\)).

3. Core Concepts:

According to Boussinesq's theory, vertical stress at depth \(z\) and horizontal distance \(x\) from a line load \(q\):

\[ \sigma_z = \dfrac{2q}{\pi z}\left[\dfrac{1}{1+(x/z)^2}\right]^2 \]

Directly below the load (\(x = 0\)):

\[\sigma_z = \dfrac{2q}{\pi z} \]

So \(\sigma_z \propto \dfrac{1}{z}\).

4. Solution Method:

\[\dfrac{\sigma_{z1}}{\sigma_{z2}} = \dfrac{2q/(\pi z_1)}{2q/(\pi z_2)} = \dfrac{z_2}{z_1} \]

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. \(z_1 = 2\text{ m}\), \(z_2 = 4\text{ m}\)
  2. \[\dfrac{\sigma_{z1}}{\sigma_{z2}} = \dfrac{4}{2} = 2.0 \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 2.0  |  Correct option: (C)

  • Given Data: Steady, incompressible, laminar flow between two infinite parallel stationary plates.
  • Aim: Determine the spatial variation (profile) of shear stress across the flow.

3. Core Concepts:

The Navier-Stokes equations simplify to:

\[\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} = \mu\dfrac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2} \]

Integrating with respect to \(y\):

\[\tau = \mu\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial y} = \left(\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x}\right)y + C \]

Applying symmetry at the center (\(y = 0\), where \(du/dy = 0\)), \(C = 0\). Thus:

\[\tau = \left(\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x}\right)y \]

Since the pressure gradient is constant, shear stress varies linearly with \(y\).

4. Solution Method:

  • At center (\(y = 0\)): \(\tau = 0\)
  • At the plates: \(\tau\) is at maximum absolute value
  • Relationship \(\tau \propto y\) is linear

6. Final Answer:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension
  • Given Data: Wastewater discharged at location S; high biodegradable organics; rate of aeration < rate of degradation (initially).
  • Aim: Determine the spatial location where dissolved oxygen (DO) is lowest.

3. Core Concepts:

The Streeter-Phelps DO Sag Curve describes two competing processes downstream of a discharge:

  • Deoxygenation: Bacteria consume DO to degrade organics (high initially due to high BOD).
  • Reaeration: Oxygen diffuses from the atmosphere (increases as DO deficit grows).

If the discharge supplied at the point A (i.e., 100) is equally divided between the pipes AB and AC, the value of \(r\) (up to two decimal places) for the pipe AC should be _______________
questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics | Pipe Networks (Hardy Cross Principles)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Head loss equation: \(h_f = rQ^{1.8}\)
    • \(r_{AB} = 1\), \(r_{BC} = 2\)
    • Inflow at A: 100 units; Outflow at B: 70 units; Outflow at C: 30 units
    • Flow at A is equally divided between pipes AB and AC
  • Aim: Find the pipe resistance \(r_{AC}\) for pipe AC.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Continuity at Nodes (Kirchhoff's 1st Law): \(\sum Q_{in} = \sum Q_{out}\) at every junction.
  • Energy Conservation in Loops (Kirchhoff's 2nd Law): The head difference between any two nodes is path-independent:
    \[H_A - H_B = \sum h_f \text{ (along any path A to B)} \]

4. Solution Method:

  1. Use equal division condition at A to find \(Q_{AB}\) and \(Q_{AC}\).
  2. Apply continuity at Node B to find \(Q_{BC}\).
  3. Apply energy conservation between A and B via both paths.
  4. Solve for \(r_{AC}\).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Flows at Node A (equally divided):
    \[Q_{AB} = Q_{AC} = \dfrac{100}{2} = 50\text{ units} \]
  2. Flow in BC (continuity at Node B):
    Inflow to B from AB = 50; required outflow = 70 \(\implies\) additional inflow needed = 20.
    \[Q_{CB} = 20\text{ units (C to B)} \]
    Self-check at C: inflow = 50, outflow = 30 (external) + 20 (to B) = 50 ✓
  3. Energy balance (A to B via two paths):
    \[h_{f,AB} = h_{f,AC} + h_{f,CB} \]\[r_{AB}(Q_{AB})^{1.8} = r_{AC}(Q_{AC})^{1.8} + r_{BC}(Q_{CB})^{1.8} \]\[1 \times (50)^{1.8} = r_{AC} \times (50)^{1.8} + 2 \times (20)^{1.8} \]\[1148.698 = 1148.698\,r_{AC} + 2 \times 218.673 \]\[1148.698 = 1148.698\,r_{AC} + 437.346 \]\[r_{AC} = \dfrac{1148.698 - 437.346}{1148.698} = \dfrac{711.352}{1148.698} \approx 0.62 \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 0.62  |  Accepted key range: 0.60 to 0.63

questions.title: GATE CE 2017 Set 1 | CE Q27

questions.question: The solution of the equation \(\dfrac{dQ}{dt} + Q = 1\) with \(Q = 0\) at \(t = 0\) is
questions.explanation:
Engineering Mathematics | Ordinary Differential Equations

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Linear ODE: \(\dfrac{dQ}{dt} + Q = 1\)
    • Initial Boundary Condition: \(Q = 0\) at \(t = 0\)
  • Aim: Find the particular solution \(Q(t)\) satisfying the ODE and the boundary condition.

3. Core Concepts:

The given equation is a first-order linear ODE of the standard form:

\[\dfrac{dy}{dt} + P(t)y = R(t) \]
  • Integrating Factor (IF): \(IF = e^{\int P(t)\, dt}\)
  • General Solution: \(y \times IF = \int (R(t) \times IF)\, dt + C\)

Alternatively, since variables are easily separable, the Variable Separable Method is used here.

4. Solution Method:

  • Rearrange to isolate \(Q\) terms on one side and \(t\) on the other.
  • Integrate both sides.
  • Apply the initial boundary condition to solve for the constant of integration \(C\).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Separate the variables:
    \[\dfrac{dQ}{dt} = 1 - Q \implies \dfrac{dQ}{1 - Q} = dt \]
  2. Integrate both sides:
    \[\int \dfrac{1}{1 - Q}\, dQ = \int 1\, dt \]\[-\ln|1 - Q| = t + C \]
  3. Apply the initial condition \(Q(0) = 0\):
    \[-\ln|1 - 0| = 0 + C \implies -\ln(1) = C \implies C = 0 \]
  4. Formulate the final solution:
    \[-\ln(1 - Q) = t \implies \ln(1 - Q) = -t \]\[1 - Q = e^{-t} \implies Q(t) = 1 - e^{-t} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: \(Q(t) = 1 - e^{-t}\)  |  Correct option: (D)

  • Substitute the eigenvalue into \((A - \lambda I)X = 0\) to find eigenvector(s).
  • Evaluate the rank of the resulting matrix to find the number of independent eigenvectors.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Find the eigenvalues:
    \[|A - \lambda I| = 0 \]\[\begin{vmatrix} 5 - \lambda & -1 \\ 4 & 1 - \lambda \end{vmatrix} = 0 \]\[(5 - \lambda)(1 - \lambda) + 4 = 0 \]\[\lambda^2 - 6\lambda + 9 = 0 \implies (\lambda - 3)^2 = 0 \implies \lambda = 3, 3 \]
    Eigenvalue \(\lambda = 3\) has an algebraic multiplicity of 2.
  2. Find the eigenvectors for \(\lambda = 3\):
    Solve \((A - 3I)X = 0\):
    \[\begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ 4 & -2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \]
    Row 2 is a multiple of Row 1, so there is only one independent equation: \(2x_1 - x_2 = 0 \implies x_2 = 2x_1\).
    Letting \(x_1 = k\), the eigenvector is \(X = k\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}\).
  3. Evaluate geometric multiplicity:
    \(\text{Rank}(A - 3I) = 1\)
    \[\text{Independent Eigenvectors} = n - \text{Rank} = 2 - 1 = 1 \]
    Thus, there is only one independent eigenvector for \(\lambda = 3\).

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: Eigenvalue 3 has algebraic multiplicity 2, and only one independent eigenvector exists.  |  Correct option: (A)

questions.question: A 1 m wide rectangular channel has a bed slope of 0.0016 and the Manning’s roughness coefficient is 0.04. Uniform flow takes place in the channel at a flow depth of 0.5 m. At a particular section, gradually varied flow (GVF) is observed and the flow depth is measured as 0.6 m. The GVF profile at that section is classified as
questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics | Open Channel Flow (GVF)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Channel width \(B = 1\text{ m}\) (Rectangular)
    • Bed slope \(S_0 = 0.0016\)
    • Manning's roughness coefficient \(n = 0.04\)
    • Normal depth \(y_n = 0.5\text{ m}\)
    • Observed GVF flow depth \(y = 0.6\text{ m}\)
  • Aim: Classify the Gradually Varied Flow (GVF) profile.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Manning's Equation for Uniform Flow: \(Q = \dfrac{1}{n} A R^{2/3} S_0^{1/2}\)
  • Critical Depth for Rectangular Channel: \(y_c = \left(\dfrac{q^2}{g}\right)^{1/3}\)
  • Slope Classification:
    • Mild (M): \(y_n > y_c\)
    • Steep (S): \(y_c > y_n\)
  • Zone Classification:
    • Zone 1: Actual depth \(y > y_n\) and \(y > y_c\)
    • Zone 2: Actual depth \(y\) is between \(y_n\) and \(y_c\)
    • Zone 3: Actual depth \(y < y_n\) and \(y < y_c\)

4. Solution Method:

  • Use normal depth and Manning's formula to calculate uniform discharge \(Q\) and unit discharge \(q\).
  • Calculate critical depth \(y_c\) using the computed \(q\).
  • Compare \(y_n\) and \(y_c\) to determine slope class (M or S).
  • Compare actual depth \(y\) with \(y_n\) and \(y_c\) to locate the zone (1, 2, or 3).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Channel properties at normal depth (\(y_n = 0.5\text{ m}\)):
    \[A = B \times y_n = 1 \times 0.5 = 0.5\text{ m}^2 \]\[P = B + 2y_n = 1 + 1 = 2.0\text{ m} \]\[R = \dfrac{A}{P} = \dfrac{0.5}{2.0} = 0.25\text{ m} \]
  2. Calculate uniform discharge \(Q\) and unit discharge \(q\):
    \[Q = \dfrac{1}{0.04} \times 0.5 \times (0.25)^{2/3} \times (0.0016)^{1/2} \]\[Q = 25 \times 0.5 \times 0.39685 \times 0.04 \approx 0.1984\text{ m}^3/\text{s} \]\[q = \dfrac{Q}{B} = 0.1984\text{ m}^2/\text{s} \]
  3. Calculate Critical Depth (\(y_c\)):
    \[y_c = \left(\dfrac{q^2}{g}\right)^{1/3} = \left(\dfrac{0.1984^2}{9.81}\right)^{1/3} = \left(\dfrac{0.03936}{9.81}\right)^{1/3} \approx 0.1589\text{ m} \]
  4. Determine Slope and Zone:
    • \(y_n (0.5\text{ m}) > y_c (0.1589\text{ m})\) \(\implies\) Mild slope (M)
    • \(y (0.6\text{ m}) > y_n (0.5\text{ m}) > y_c (0.1589\text{ m})\) \(\implies\) Actual depth lies above both normal and critical depths \(\implies\) Zone 1
    Therefore, the profile is classified as \(M_1\).

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: Profile is classified as \(M_1\)  |  Correct option: (C)

QR108°15'RQ286°15'

questions.explanation:
Geomatics | Surveying - Compass Surveying

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis & Evaluation
  • Given Data: Observed Fore Bearings (FB) and Back Bearings (BB) for a traverse.
  • Aim: Identify which station(s) are most likely affected by local attraction.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Local Attraction: A magnetic anomaly at a station that uniformly deflects the magnetic needle.
  • Detection: If \(|\text{FB} - \text{BB}| = 180^\circ 00'\) for a line, both end stations of that line are considered free from local attraction.
  • Consistency Principle: The error caused by local attraction at any specific station must be a constant value for all bearings observed from that station.

4. Solution Method & Error Detection:

Evaluate the FB–BB differences for all lines:

  • Line PQ: FB \(= 46^\circ 15'\), BB \(= 226^\circ 15'\) \(\implies |226^\circ 15' - 46^\circ 15'| = 180^\circ 00'\) — Stations P and Q appear free from local attraction.
  • Line ST: FB \(= 321^\circ 45'\), BB \(= 141^\circ 45'\) \(\implies |321^\circ 45' - 141^\circ 45'| = 180^\circ 00'\) — Stations S and T appear free from local attraction.

Checking for physical consistency at Station R:

  1. Via Q (free station):
    • Correct FB of QR = Observed FB \(= 108^\circ 15'\)
    • Correct BB of QR \(= 108^\circ 15' + 180^\circ = 288^\circ 15'\)
    • Observed BB of QR (from R) \(= 286^\circ 15'\)
    • Local attraction error at R \(= 286^\circ 15' - 288^\circ 15' = -2^\circ 00'\)
  2. Via S (free station):
    • Correct BB of RS (from S) = Observed BB \(= 20^\circ 30'\)
    • Correct FB of RS (from R) \(= 20^\circ 30' + 180^\circ = 200^\circ 30'\)
    • Observed FB of RS \(= 201^\circ 30'\)
    • Local attraction error at R \(= 201^\circ 30' - 200^\circ 30' = +1^\circ 00'\)

The required correction at Station R is \(-2^\circ\) via line QR, but \(+1^\circ\) via line RS. Since local attraction represents a single magnetic deviation at a fixed location, the error must be uniform for all readings taken from that station. The data is therefore physically inconsistent — no single set of local attractions can produce these readings. GATE authorities recognized this critical flaw and awarded Marks to All for this question.

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: Data is physically inconsistent (error at R evaluates to both \(-2^\circ\) and \(+1^\circ\)).  |  Correct option: Marks to All

questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.question: Consider the equation \(\dfrac{du}{dt} = 3t^2 + 1\) with \(u = 0\) at \(t = 0\). This is numerically solved by using the forward Euler method with a step size, \(\Delta t = 2\). The absolute error in the solution at the end of the first time step is _______________
questions.explanation:
Engineering Mathematics | Numerical Methods - Differential Equations

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • ODE: \(\dfrac{du}{dt} = 3t^2 + 1\)
    • Initial condition: \(u(0) = 0\)
    • Numerical method: Forward Euler Method
    • Step size: \(\Delta t = 2\)
  • Aim: Find the absolute error in the solution at the end of the first time step (\(t = 2\)).

3. Core Concepts:

  • Exact (Analytical) Solution: Found by integrating the ODE using the initial boundary conditions.
  • Forward Euler Method: A first-order numerical procedure.
    \[u_{n+1} = u_n + f(t_n,\, u_n)\, \Delta t \]
  • Absolute Error: \(|\text{Exact Value} - \text{Approximate Value}|\)

4. Solution Method:

  1. Integrate the ODE to find exact \(u(t)\); evaluate at \(t = 2\).
  2. Apply one iteration of the Forward Euler formula from \(t_0 = 0\) to find the numerical approximation at \(t = 2\).
  3. Calculate the absolute difference.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Exact Analytical Solution:
    \[\int du = \int (3t^2 + 1)\, dt \implies u(t) = t^3 + t + C \]Applying \(u(0) = 0\): \(C = 0\), so \(u(t) = t^3 + t\).
    At \(t = 2\):
    \[u_{exact}(2) = 2^3 + 2 = 10 \]
  2. Numerical Approximation (Euler's Method):
    \(f(t, u) = 3t^2 + 1\), \(\quad t_0 = 0\), \(\quad u_0 = 0\), \(\quad \Delta t = 2\)
    \[f(t_0, u_0) = 3(0)^2 + 1 = 1 \]\[u_1 = u_0 + f(t_0, u_0)\,\Delta t = 0 + (1)(2) = 2 \]
  3. Absolute Error:
    \[\text{Error} = |u_{exact} - u_{approx}| = |10 - 2| = 8 \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 8.00  |  Accepted key range: 7.95 to 8.05

questions.title: GATE CE 2017 Set 1 | CE Q38
questions.subject: Concrete & Steel Structures
questions.topic: Limit State Design of Beams & Slabs
questions.question: A pre-tensioned rectangular concrete beam 150 mm wide and 300 mm depth is prestressed with three straight tendons, each having a cross-sectional area of 50 mm², to an initial stress of 1200 N/mm². The tendons are located at 100 mm from the soffit of the beam. If the modular ratio is 6, the loss of prestressing force (in kN, up to one decimal place) due to the elastic deformation of concrete only is _______________
questions.explanation:
Structural Engineering | Prestressed Concrete - Losses

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Pre-tensioned beam: \(b = 150\text{ mm}\), \(D = 300\text{ mm}\)
    • Tendons: 3 cables, area per cable \(= 50\text{ mm}^2\) \(\implies\) Total steel area \(A_{ps} = 150\text{ mm}^2\)
    • Initial stress in steel: \(f_{pi} = 1200\text{ N/mm}^2\)
    • Tendon location: \(100\text{ mm}\) from soffit
    • Modular ratio: \(m = 6\)
  • Aim: Calculate the loss of prestressing force due to elastic deformation of concrete (in kN).

3. Core Concepts:

  • Eccentricity (\(e\)): Distance from the centroidal axis of the section to the level of steel.
  • Initial Prestressing Force (\(P_i\)): \(P_i = A_{ps} \times f_{pi}\)
  • Stress in Concrete at Steel Level (\(f_c\)): Due to initial prestress force on the gross section (IS 1343 practice for pre-tensioned elements):
    \[f_c = \dfrac{P_i}{A} + \dfrac{P_i \cdot e^2}{I} \]
  • Elastic Shortening Loss:
    \[\Delta f_p = m \cdot f_c \qquad \Delta P = \Delta f_p \times A_{ps} \]

4. Solution Method:

  1. Determine cross-sectional properties (\(A\), \(I\), \(e\)).
  2. Calculate initial prestressing force \(P_i\).
  3. Calculate concrete stress \(f_c\) at the level of tendons.
  4. Multiply \(f_c\) by modular ratio \(m\) to get stress loss in steel.
  5. Multiply stress loss by total steel area to get force loss; convert to kN.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Section Properties:
    \[A = 150 \times 300 = 45{,}000\text{ mm}^2 \]\[I = \dfrac{150 \times 300^3}{12} = 337{,}500{,}000\text{ mm}^4 \]\[y_b = \dfrac{300}{2} = 150\text{ mm} \quad \implies \quad e = 150 - 100 = 50\text{ mm} \]
  2. Initial Prestressing Force:
    \[P_i = 150 \times 1200 = 180{,}000\text{ N} \]
  3. Concrete stress at tendon level (\(f_c\)):
    \[f_c = \dfrac{180{,}000}{45{,}000} + \dfrac{180{,}000 \times (50)^2}{337{,}500{,}000} \]\[f_c = 4.0 + \dfrac{450{,}000{,}000}{337{,}500{,}000} = 4.0 + 1.333 = 5.333\text{ N/mm}^2 \]
  4. Loss in Prestressing Force:
    \[\Delta f_p = m \times f_c = 6 \times 5.333 = 32.0\text{ N/mm}^2 \]\[\Delta P = 32.0 \times 150 = 4800\text{ N} = 4.8\text{ kN} \]
    Note: If calculated using the exact transformed section area \(A_e\), the answer is \(4.73\text{ kN}\). The GATE key accepts a range accommodating both standard methods.

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 4.8 kN  |  Accepted key range: 4.5 to 5.0

questions.title: GATE CE 2017 Set 1 | CE Q39
questions.subject: Structural Analysis & Mechanics
questions.question:
Consider the stepped bar made with a linear elastic material and subjected to an axial load of 1 kN, as shown in the figure.

Segments 1 and 2 have cross-sectional area of 100 mm² and 60 mm², Young’s modulus of 2×10⁵ MPa and 3×10⁵ MPa, and length of 400 mm and 900 mm, respectively. The strain energy (in N-mm, up to one decimal place) in the bar due to the axial load is _______________
questions.explanation:
Solid Mechanics | Strain Energy

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Axial Load: \(P = 1\text{ kN} = 1000\text{ N}\)
    • Segment 1: \(A_1 = 100\text{ mm}^2\), \(E_1 = 2 \times 10^5\text{ N/mm}^2\), \(L_1 = 400\text{ mm}\)
    • Segment 2: \(A_2 = 60\text{ mm}^2\), \(E_2 = 3 \times 10^5\text{ N/mm}^2\), \(L_2 = 900\text{ mm}\)
  • Aim: Calculate the total strain energy (in N-mm) stored in the stepped bar.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Strain Energy in Axial Loading: The elastic strain energy stored in a uniform bar under axial load \(P\):
    \[U = \dfrac{P^2 L}{2AE} \]
  • Principle of Superposition: For a stepped bar in series, the total strain energy is the sum of individual segment energies. Since the load is applied at the free end, the internal axial force in both segments equals \(P\).
    \[U_{total} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \dfrac{P_i^2 L_i}{2 A_i E_i} \]

4. Solution Method:

  1. Verify units: load in N, lengths in mm, modulus in MPa (N/mm²) — resulting strain energy will be in N-mm.
  2. Calculate strain energy for Segment 1 (\(U_1\)).
  3. Calculate strain energy for Segment 2 (\(U_2\)).
  4. Add both values for total strain energy.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Calculate \(U_1\) for Segment 1:
    \[U_1 = \dfrac{(1000)^2 \times 400}{2 \times 100 \times (2 \times 10^5)} = \dfrac{4 \times 10^8}{4 \times 10^7} = 10\text{ N-mm} \]
  2. Calculate \(U_2\) for Segment 2:
    \[U_2 = \dfrac{(1000)^2 \times 900}{2 \times 60 \times (3 \times 10^5)} = \dfrac{9 \times 10^8}{3.6 \times 10^7} = 25\text{ N-mm} \]
  3. Total Strain Energy:
    \[U_{total} = U_1 + U_2 = 10 + 25 = 35\text{ N-mm} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 35.0 N-mm  |  Accepted key range: 34.9 to 35.1

questions.title: GATE CE 2017 Set 1 | CE Q40
questions.subject: Structural Analysis & Mechanics
questions.question:
The value of M in the beam ABC shown in the figure is such that the joint B does not rotate.

The value of support reaction (in kN) at B should be equal to _______________
questions.explanation:
Structural Analysis | Slope and Deflection

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Beam ABC: fixed support at A, roller at B, roller at C
    • Span AB \(= 4\text{ m}\), Span BC \(= 6\text{ m}\)
    • UDL \(w = 30\text{ kN/m}\) over span AB
    • Concentrated moment \(M\) applied at joint B
    • Kinematic condition: \(\theta_B = 0\) (joint B does not rotate)
  • Aim: Find the support reaction at B (\(R_B\)) in kN.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Kinematic Constraints: The condition \(\theta_B = 0\) implies the beam behaves exactly as if B is a fixed support, decoupling the beam into two independent spans — Span AB (Fixed-Fixed) and Span BC (Fixed-Pinned).
  • Fixed-End Reactions: For a fixed-fixed beam under UDL \(w\) over length \(L\), symmetry gives:
    \[V = \dfrac{wL}{2} \]
  • Moment Equilibrium at Joint: The external moment \(M\) maintains \(\theta_B = 0\) and does not induce additional vertical shear in the spans.

4. Solution Method:

  1. Analyze Span AB as a fixed-fixed beam; calculate vertical reaction at B from this span (\(V_{BL}\)).
  2. Analyze Span BC — no external loads, so vertical reaction at B from this span (\(V_{BR}\)) is zero.
  3. Sum shear forces from both spans for total \(R_B\).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Reaction from Span AB (\(V_{BL}\)):
    \[V_{BL} = \dfrac{wL_{AB}}{2} = \dfrac{30 \times 4}{2} = 60\text{ kN} \]Note: Fixed-end moments \(M_{AB} = M_{BA} = \dfrac{wL^2}{12} = 40\text{ kN-m}\) satisfy internal bending mechanics but do not alter the vertical shear due to symmetry.
  2. Reaction from Span BC (\(V_{BR}\)):
    No transverse loading on span BC \(\implies V_{BR} = 0\text{ kN}\)
  3. Total Support Reaction at B:
    \[R_B = V_{BL} + V_{BR} = 60 + 0 = 60\text{ kN} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 60.0 kN  |  Accepted key range: 59.0 to 61.0

questions.title: GATE CE 2017 Set 1 | CE Q41
questions.subject: Structural Analysis & Mechanics
questions.question:
Consider the beam ABCD shown in the figure.

For a moving concentrated load of 50 kN on the beam, the magnitude of the maximum bending moment (in kN-m) obtained at the support C will be equal to _______________
questions.explanation:
Structural Analysis | Influence Line Diagrams (ILD)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Beam ABCD: pin support at A, internal hinge at B, roller supports at C and D
    • \(AB = 4\text{ m}\), \(BC = 4\text{ m}\), \(CD = 10\text{ m}\)
    • Moving concentrated load \(P = 50\text{ kN}\)
  • Aim: Find the magnitude of the maximum bending moment (in kN-m) at support C.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Static Determinacy: The internal hinge at B separates the structure into a simply supported span AB (resting on A and B) and an overhanging simply supported span BCD (supported at C and D).
  • ILD for Bending Moment at C: The moment at C is maximized when the moving load creates the maximum lever arm effect. Placing the load at internal hinge B transfers the entire load to the tip of the overhang BC.

4. Solution Method:

  1. Determine the expression for \(M_C\) depending on load position.
  2. Note: loads on CD produce \(M_C = 0\) (BCD acts as a simple span for loads on CD).
  3. Worst-case hogging moment at C occurs when the load is on the overhanging segment — maximum lever arm is achieved when load is at hinge B.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Load at Internal Hinge B:
    When the \(50\text{ kN}\) load acts at B, the reaction of span AB at B is \(50\text{ kN}\). This force acts as a downward point load on the overhang BC at a distance of \(4\text{ m}\) from support C.
  2. Calculate Bending Moment at C:
    Taking moments of all forces to the left of C:
    \[M_C = -(\text{Load at B}) \times L_{BC} = -50 \times 4 = -200\text{ kN-m} \]
  3. Maximum Magnitude:
    \[|M_C|_{max} = |-200| = 200\text{ kN-m} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 200 kN-m  |  Accepted key range: 199 to 201

questions.title: GATE CE 2017 Set 1 | CE Q42
questions.subject: Structural Analysis & Mechanics
questions.question: Consider two axially loaded columns, namely, 1 and 2, made of a linear elastic material with Young’s modulus 2×10⁵ MPa, square cross-section with side 10 mm, and length 1 m. For Column 1, one end is fixed and the other end is free. For Column 2, one end is fixed and the other end is pinned. Based on the Euler’s theory, the ratio (up to one decimal place) of the buckling load of Column 2 to the buckling load of Column 1 is _______________
questions.explanation:
Solid Mechanics | Columns / Buckling

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension / Application
  • Given Data:
    • Both columns: \(E = 2 \times 10^5\text{ MPa}\), square cross-section \(10\text{ mm} \times 10\text{ mm}\), length \(L = 1\text{ m}\)
    • Column 1: Fixed-Free end conditions
    • Column 2: Fixed-Pinned end conditions
    • Theory: Euler's buckling theory
  • Aim: Find the ratio of the buckling load of Column 2 to Column 1.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Euler's Critical Buckling Load:
    \[P_{cr} = \dfrac{\pi^2 EI}{L_{eff}^2} \]where \(L_{eff}\) is the effective length of the column.
  • Theoretical Effective Lengths:
    End Condition\(L_{eff}\) (Theoretical)
    Fixed-Free (Column 1)\(2L\)
    Fixed-Pinned (Column 2)\(L/\sqrt{2}\)
    Note: IS 800 recommends \(0.8L\) for Fixed-Pinned in design, but the question explicitly requires the theoretical Euler's value.

4. Solution Method:

Since \(E\), \(I\), and \(L\) are identical for both columns, the ratio of buckling loads is inversely proportional to the square of their effective lengths:

\[\text{Ratio} = \dfrac{P_{cr2}}{P_{cr1}} = \dfrac{L_{eff1}^2}{L_{eff2}^2} \]

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Express effective lengths:
    \[L_{eff1} = 2L, \qquad L_{eff2} = \dfrac{L}{\sqrt{2}} \]
  2. Calculate the ratio:
    \[\dfrac{P_{cr2}}{P_{cr1}} = \dfrac{(2L)^2}{\left(\dfrac{L}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^2} = \dfrac{4L^2}{L^2/2} = 4 \times 2 = 8.0 \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 8.0  |  Accepted key range: 7.9 to 8.3

questions.title: GATE CE 2017 Set 1 | CE Q43
questions.subject: Concrete & Steel Structures
questions.topic: Steel Tension, Compression Members & Plastic Analysis
questions.question:
A column is subjected to a load through a bracket as shown in the figure.

The resultant force (in kN, up to one decimal place) in the bolt 1 is _______________
questions.explanation:
Steel Structures | Eccentric Bolted Connection

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • \(P = 10\text{ kN}\) (downward)
    • 4 bolts in a square pattern, horizontal & vertical spacing \(= 100\text{ mm}\)
    • Eccentricity \(e = 150\text{ mm}\) from bolt group CG to load \(P\)
    • Bolt 1 is the top-left bolt
  • Aim: Find the resultant force in Bolt 1.

3. Core Concepts:

  • In-Plane Eccentric Connection (IS 800:2007 Sec 10.5): A bolt experiences:
    • Direct Shear (\(F_d\)): \(F_d = P/n\) — acts uniformly downward.
    • Torsional Shear (\(F_t\)): \(F_t = M \cdot r\,/\,\sum r^2\) — acts perpendicular to the radius vector from the CG.
  • Resultant Force:
    \[F_R = \sqrt{F_d^2 + F_t^2 + 2F_d F_t \cos\theta} \]

4. Error Handling & Correction Protocol:

A rigorous mechanical evaluation yields \(F_R = 3.95\text{ kN}\), but the official GATE answer key mandates \(6.0\text{ kN}\).

Identified Error in Key Generation: The examiner incorrectly used \(r = 50\text{ mm}\) (the \(x\) or \(y\) coordinate alone) instead of the true geometric radius \(r = \sqrt{50^2 + 50^2} = 70.71\text{ mm}\), and used \(\sum r^2 = 4 \times 50^2 = 10{,}000\text{ mm}^2\) instead of \(20{,}000\text{ mm}^2\). This artificially inflated \(F_t\) to \(7.5\text{ kN}\).

Both approaches are shown below.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

Part A: Mathematically Correct Approach

  1. Geometric Properties:
    CG at \((0,0)\); Bolt 1 at \((-50,\ 50)\).
    True radius: \(r = \sqrt{50^2 + 50^2} = 50\sqrt{2} \approx 70.71\text{ mm}\)
    \(\sum r^2 = 4 \times (50\sqrt{2})^2 = 20{,}000\text{ mm}^2\)
  2. Direct Shear:
    \[F_d = \dfrac{10}{4} = 2.5\text{ kN (downward)} \]
  3. Torsional Shear:
    \[M = P \times e = 10 \times 150 = 1500\text{ kN-mm} \]\[F_t = \dfrac{1500 \times 50\sqrt{2}}{20{,}000} \approx 5.303\text{ kN} \]
  4. Vector Addition:
    Radius vector of Bolt 1 is at \(135^\circ\). Clockwise moment pushes \(F_t\) up and to the right (\(45^\circ\) to horizontal). Angle between \(F_d\) (downward) and \(F_t\) is \(135^\circ\).
    \[F_R = \sqrt{2.5^2 + 5.303^2 + 2(2.5)(5.303)\cos(135^\circ)} \approx 3.95\text{ kN} \]

Part B: GATE Key Approach (Flawed Geometry)

  1. Flawed Properties: \(r = 50\text{ mm}\), \(\sum r^2 = 10{,}000\text{ mm}^2\)
  2. Inflated Torsional Shear:
    \[F_{t(wrong)} = \dfrac{1500 \times 50}{10{,}000} = 7.5\text{ kN} \]
  3. Flawed Resultant (using \(\theta = 135^\circ\)):
    \[F_R = \sqrt{2.5^2 + 7.5^2 + 2(2.5)(7.5)\cos(135^\circ)} \]\[= \sqrt{6.25 + 56.25 - 26.51} = \sqrt{35.99} \approx 6.0\text{ kN} \]

6. Final Answer:

True value: 3.95 kN  |  Accepted key range: 5.9 to 6.1 (due to the documented framing error by the examiner)

questions.title: GATE CE 2017 Set 1 | CE Q44
questions.subject: Structural Analysis & Mechanics
questions.question: A particle of mass 2 kg is travelling at a velocity of 1.5 m/s. A force f(t) = 3t² (in N) is applied to it in the direction of motion for a duration of 2 seconds, where t denotes time in seconds. The velocity (in m/s, up to one decimal place) of the particle immediately after the removal of the force is _______________
questions.explanation:
Engineering Mechanics | Kinematics & Dynamics

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Mass: \(m = 2\text{ kg}\)
    • Initial velocity: \(u = 1.5\text{ m/s}\)
    • Applied force: \(F(t) = 3t^2\text{ N}\)
    • Duration: \(\Delta t = 2\text{ s}\) (from \(t = 0\) to \(t = 2\))
  • Aim: Find the final velocity (\(v\)) immediately after the force is removed.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Newton's Second Law:
    \[F = \dfrac{dp}{dt} = m\dfrac{dv}{dt} \]
  • Impulse-Momentum Theorem: The integral of force over the time interval equals the change in momentum.
    \[J = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} F(t)\, dt = \Delta p = m(v - u) \]

4. Solution Method:

  1. Integrate \(F(t)\) over the given time limits to find total impulse \(J\).
  2. Equate the impulse to the change in momentum.
  3. Solve for final velocity \(v\).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Calculate total impulse (\(J\)):
    \[ J = \int_{0}^{2} 3t^2\, dt = 3\left[\dfrac{t^3}{3}\right]_{0}^{2} = \left[t^3\right]_{0}^{2} = 8\text{ N·s} \]
  2. Apply the Impulse-Momentum Theorem:
    \[J = m(v - u) \implies 8 = 2(v - 1.5) \]
  3. Solve for \(v\):
    \[v - 1.5 = \dfrac{8}{2} = 4 \implies v = 5.5\text{ m/s} \]
    Sanity Check: The force is strictly positive and in the direction of motion, so \(v > u\). \(5.5 > 1.5\) ✓

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 5.5 m/s  |  Accepted key range: 5.4 to 5.6

questions.title: GATE CE 2017 Set 1 | CE Q45
questions.subject: Concrete & Steel Structures
questions.question:
The activity details of a project are given below:
ActivityDepends onDuration (in days)
P--6
QP15
RQ, T12
SR16

UQ, T14
VU16
The estimated minimum time (in days) for the completion of the project will be _______________
questions.explanation:
Construction Management | Project Management (CPM/PERT)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application & Analysis
  • Given Data: A project network with 7 activities (P, Q, R, S, T, U, V), their predecessor dependencies, and respective durations.
  • Aim: Estimate the minimum project completion time (duration of the critical path).

3. Core Concepts:

  • Critical Path Method (CPM): The minimum time to complete a project is dictated by the longest continuous sequence of activities from start to finish — the Critical Path.
  • Network Logic: Activities without predecessors start at time 0. A successor can only begin after all its predecessors are complete.

4. Solution Method:

Trace all possible distinct paths from start to finish and compute their cumulative durations. The maximum duration is the minimum project completion time.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Map out dependencies:
    • Start \(\rightarrow\) P (no predecessor)
    • P \(\rightarrow\) Q and P \(\rightarrow\) T
    • (Q, T) \(\rightarrow\) R and (Q, T) \(\rightarrow\) U
    • R \(\rightarrow\) S \(\rightarrow\) End
    • U \(\rightarrow\) V \(\rightarrow\) End
  2. All valid paths and their durations:
    PathSequenceDuration (days)
    1P → Q → R → S\(6 + 15 + 12 + 16 = 49\)
    2P → T → R → S\(6 + 10 + 12 + 16 = 44\)
    3P → Q → U → V\(6 + 15 + 14 + 16 = 51\)
    4P → T → U → V\(6 + 10 + 14 + 16 = 46\)
  3. Critical Path: Path 3 has the maximum duration of 51 days.

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 51 days  |  Accepted key range: 51 to 51

questions.title: GATE CE 2017 Set 1 | CE Q46
questions.subject: Geotechnical Engineering (Soil)
questions.question: It is proposed to drive H-piles up to a depth of 7 m at a construction site. The average surface area of the H-pile is 3 m² per meter length. The soil at the site is homogeneous sand, having an effective friction angle of 32°. The ground water table (GWT) is at a depth of 2 m below the ground surface. The unit weights of the soil above and below the GWT are 16 kN/m³ and 19 kN/m³, respectively. Assume the earth pressure coefficient, K = 1.0, and the angle of wall friction, δ = 23°. The total axial frictional resistance (in kN, up to one decimal place) mobilized on the pile against the driving is _______________
questions.explanation:
Geotechnical Engineering | Deep Foundations (Pile Foundation)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application & Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Pile length: \(L = 7\text{ m}\)
    • Pile perimeter: \(P = 3\text{ m}\) (surface area \(= 3\text{ m}^2/\text{m}\))
    • Depth of GWT \(= 2\text{ m}\)
    • Bulk unit weight above GWT: \(\gamma_{bulk} = 16\text{ kN/m}^3\)
    • Saturated unit weight below GWT: \(\gamma_{sat} = 19\text{ kN/m}^3\)
    • Earth pressure coefficient: \(K = 1.0\)
    • Angle of wall friction: \(\delta = 23^\circ\)
  • Aim: Calculate the total axial frictional resistance (\(Q_s\)) along the pile shaft.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Skin Friction in Sand (IS 2911):
    \[Q_s = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (K \cdot \bar{\sigma}_{vi}' \cdot \tan\delta) \cdot (P \cdot \Delta L_i) \]where \(\bar{\sigma}_{vi}'\) = average vertical effective stress in layer \(i\).
  • Submerged unit weight: \(\gamma_{sub} = \gamma_{sat} - \gamma_w\), with \(\gamma_w = 9.81\text{ kN/m}^3\).

4. Solution Method:

Divide the soil profile into two layers at the GWT interface, compute average effective vertical stress for each layer, calculate frictional resistance, and sum them.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Effective stress at key depths:
    • At \(z = 0\text{ m}\): \(\sigma_v' = 0\text{ kN/m}^2\)
    • At \(z = 2\text{ m}\): \(\sigma_v' = 16 \times 2 = 32\text{ kN/m}^2\)
    • \(\gamma_{sub} = 19 - 9.81 = 9.19\text{ kN/m}^3\)
    • At \(z = 7\text{ m}\): \(\sigma_v' = 32 + (9.19 \times 5) = 32 + 45.95 = 77.95\text{ kN/m}^2\)
  2. Layer 1 (0 to 2 m):
    \[\bar{\sigma}_{v1}' = \dfrac{0 + 32}{2} = 16\text{ kN/m}^2 \]\[f_{s1} = 1.0 \times 16 \times \tan(23^\circ) = 16 \times 0.42447 = 6.791\text{ kN/m}^2 \]\[Q_{s1} = 6.791 \times (3 \times 2) = 6.791 \times 6 = 40.75\text{ kN} \]
  3. Layer 2 (2 to 7 m):
    \[\bar{\sigma}_{v2}' = \dfrac{32 + 77.95}{2} = 54.975\text{ kN/m}^2 \]\[f_{s2} = 1.0 \times 54.975 \times \tan(23^\circ) = 54.975 \times 0.42447 = 23.335\text{ kN/m}^2 \]\[Q_{s2} = 23.335 \times (3 \times 5) = 23.335 \times 15 = 350.03\text{ kN} \]
  4. Total frictional resistance:
    \[Q_s = Q_{s1} + Q_{s2} = 40.75 + 350.03 = 390.8\text{ kN} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 390.8 kN  |  Accepted key range: 385.0 to 392.0

questions.title: GATE CE 2017 Set 1 | CE Q47
questions.subject: Geotechnical Engineering (Soil)
questions.question:
The infinite sand slope shown in the figure is on the verge of sliding failure. The ground water table coincides with the ground surface. Unit weight of water γ_w = 9.81 kN/m³.

The value of the effective angle of internal friction (in degrees, up to one decimal place) of the sand is _______________
questions.explanation:
Geotechnical Engineering | Soil Mechanics (Slope Stability)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application & Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Slope inclination: \(\beta = 20^\circ\)
    • Slope on verge of sliding: \(FS = 1.0\)
    • Water table coincides with ground surface; seepage parallel to slope
    • \(\gamma_{sat} = 21\text{ kN/m}^3\), \(\gamma_w = 9.81\text{ kN/m}^3\)
  • Aim: Find the effective angle of internal friction (\(\phi'\)) of the sand.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Infinite Slope with Parallel Seepage: When seepage extends up to the ground surface, pore pressures reduce the effective normal stress on the failure plane. The factor of safety is:
    \[FS = \dfrac{\gamma_{sub}}{\gamma_{sat}} \cdot \dfrac{\tan\phi'}{\tan\beta} \]where \(\gamma_{sub} = \gamma_{sat} - \gamma_w\).

4. Solution Method:

Enforce limiting equilibrium (\(FS = 1.0\)) and rearrange the infinite slope equation to solve directly for \(\phi'\).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Calculate submerged unit weight:
    \[\gamma_{sub} = 21 - 9.81 = 11.19\text{ kN/m}^3 \]
  2. Apply limiting equilibrium:
    \[1.0 = \dfrac{11.19}{21} \times \dfrac{\tan\phi'}{\tan 20^\circ} \]
  3. Solve for \(\phi'\):
    \[\tan 20^\circ = 0.36397 \]\[\tan\phi' = \dfrac{0.36397}{11.19/21} = \dfrac{0.36397}{0.53286} = 0.68305 \]\[\phi' = \arctan(0.68305) \approx 34.3^\circ \]
    Sanity Check: \(\phi' \approx 34^\circ\) is a typical realistic value for medium-dense sand. ✓

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 34.3°  |  Accepted key range: 34.0 to 34.5

questions.title: GATE CE 2017 Set 1 | CE Q48
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question:
A sluice gate used to control the flow in a horizontal channel of unit width is shown in the figure.

It is observed that the depth of flow is 1.0 m upstream of the gate, while the depth is 0.2 m downstream of the gate. Assuming a smooth flow transition across the sluice gate, i.e., without any energy loss, and the acceleration due to gravity as 10 m/s², the discharge (in m³/s, up to two decimal places) passing under the sluice gate is _______________
questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics | Open Channel Flow (Specific Energy)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Upstream flow depth: \(d_1 = 1.0\text{ m}\)
    • Downstream flow depth: \(d_2 = 0.2\text{ m}\)
    • Channel unit width: \(B = 1\text{ m}\)
    • Energy loss through gate: \(h_L = 0\) (smooth transition)
    • \(g = 10\text{ m/s}^2\)
  • Aim: Determine the volumetric discharge \(Q\) (in m³/s) passing under the sluice gate.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Specific Energy (\(E\)): Since the channel bed is horizontal, specific energy is conserved across the gate (\(E_1 = E_2\)).
    \[E = d + \dfrac{V^2}{2g} = d + \dfrac{q^2}{2gd^2} \]where \(q\) is the discharge per unit width.
  • Continuity: For a rectangular channel of constant width, \(q = V_1 d_1 = V_2 d_2\).

4. Solution Method:

Equate specific energy at sections 1 and 2, substitute the velocity term using continuity in terms of \(q\), and solve for \(q\) and hence \(Q\).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Set up specific energy balance:
    \[d_1 + \dfrac{q^2}{2g d_1^2} = d_2 + \dfrac{q^2}{2g d_2^2} \]
  2. Substitute values:
    \[1.0 + \dfrac{q^2}{20 \times 1^2} = 0.2 + \dfrac{q^2}{20 \times (0.2)^2} \]\[1.0 + \dfrac{q^2}{20} = 0.2 + \dfrac{q^2}{0.8} \]
  3. Solve algebraically for \(q\):
    \[1.0 - 0.2 = q^2\left(\dfrac{1}{0.8} - \dfrac{1}{20}\right) \]\[0.8 = q^2(1.25 - 0.05) = 1.2\, q^2 \]\[q^2 = \dfrac{0.8}{1.2} = \dfrac{2}{3} \approx 0.6667\text{ m}^4/\text{s}^2 \]\[q = \sqrt{0.6667} \approx 0.8165\text{ m}^2/\text{s} \]
  4. Total discharge:
    \[Q = q \times B = 0.8165 \times 1 \approx 0.82\text{ m}^3/\text{s} \]
    Sanity Check: \(Fr_1 = 0.8165/\sqrt{10 \times 1} = 0.26\) (subcritical upstream ✓); \(Fr_2 = (0.8165/0.2)/\sqrt{10 \times 0.2} = 2.88\) (supercritical downstream ✓).

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 0.82 m³/s  |  Accepted key range: 0.80 to 0.83

questions.title: GATE CE 2017 Set 1 | CE Q49
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question:
Water flows through a 90° bend in a horizontal plane as depicted in the figure.

A pressure of 140 kPa is measured at Section 1-1. The inlet diameter marked at Section 1-1 is \(\dfrac{27}{\sqrt{\pi}}\) cm, while the nozzle diameter marked at Section 2-2 is \(\dfrac{14}{\sqrt{\pi}}\) cm. Assume the following:
(i) Acceleration due to gravity = 10 m/s².
(ii) Weights of both the bent pipe segment as well as water are negligible.
(iii) Friction across the bend is negligible.
The magnitude of the force (in kN, up to two decimal places) that would be required to hold the pipe section is _______________
questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics | Fluid Dynamics

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application / Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Bend angle: \(90^\circ\) in a horizontal plane
    • Inlet pressure: \(P_1 = 140\text{ kPa}\) (gauge)
    • Outlet pressure: \(P_2 = 0\text{ kPa}\) (gauge, atmospheric)
    • Inlet diameter: \(D_1 = \dfrac{0.27}{\sqrt{\pi}}\text{ m}\)
    • Outlet diameter: \(D_2 = \dfrac{0.14}{\sqrt{\pi}}\text{ m}\)
    • \(g = 10\text{ m/s}^2\), \(\rho = 1000\text{ kg/m}^3\)
  • Aim: Calculate the magnitude of the external force (in kN) required to hold the pipe in place.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Continuity Equation: \(A_1 V_1 = A_2 V_2 = Q\)
  • Bernoulli's Equation (horizontal, frictionless):
    \[\dfrac{P_1}{\rho g} + \dfrac{V_1^2}{2g} = \dfrac{P_2}{\rho g} + \dfrac{V_2^2}{2g} \]
  • Linear Momentum Equation:
    \[\sum \vec{F} = \rho Q (\vec{V}_2 - \vec{V}_1) \]where \(\sum\vec{F}\) includes pressure forces and external holding forces on the control volume.

4. Solution Method:

  1. Compute areas \(A_1\) and \(A_2\); find velocity relation from continuity.
  2. Substitute into Bernoulli's equation to solve for \(V_1\) and \(V_2\).
  3. Calculate mass flow rate \(\dot{m}\).
  4. Apply momentum equation in X and Y directions to find \(F_{hold,X}\) and \(F_{hold,Y}\).
  5. Compute resultant: \(F = \sqrt{F_X^2 + F_Y^2}\).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Areas and velocity relation:
    \[A_1 = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\left(\dfrac{0.27}{\sqrt{\pi}}\right)^2 = \dfrac{0.27^2}{4} = 0.018225\text{ m}^2 \]\[A_2 = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\left(\dfrac{0.14}{\sqrt{\pi}}\right)^2 = \dfrac{0.14^2}{4} = 0.0049\text{ m}^2 \]\[V_2 = \dfrac{A_1}{A_2}\,V_1 = \dfrac{0.018225}{0.0049}\,V_1 \approx 3.7194\,V_1 \]
  2. Bernoulli's equation:
    \[14 + \dfrac{V_1^2}{20} = \dfrac{(3.7194\,V_1)^2}{20} \]\[280 + V_1^2 = 13.8338\,V_1^2 \implies V_1^2 = 21.817 \implies V_1 = 4.671\text{ m/s} \]\[V_2 = 3.7194 \times 4.671 = 17.373\text{ m/s} \]
  3. Discharge and mass flow rate:
    \[Q = A_1 V_1 = 0.018225 \times 4.671 = 0.08513\text{ m}^3/\text{s} \]\[\dot{m} = 1000 \times 0.08513 = 85.13\text{ kg/s} \]
  4. Momentum equation (inlet along \(+\hat{j}\), outlet along \(+\hat{i}\)):
    X-direction:\[F_X = \dot{m}V_2 = 85.13 \times 17.373 = 1478.96\text{ N} = 1.479\text{ kN} \]Y-direction:\[F_Y + P_1 A_1 = -\dot{m}V_1 \]\[F_Y + (140{,}000 \times 0.018225) = -(85.13 \times 4.671) \]\[F_Y + 2551.5 = -397.6 \implies F_Y = -2949.1\text{ N} = -2.949\text{ kN} \]
  5. Resultant force:
    \[|\vec{F}_{hold}| = \sqrt{1.479^2 + (-2.949)^2} = \sqrt{2.187 + 8.697} = 3.30\text{ kN} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 3.30 kN  |  Accepted key range: 2.50 to 3.75

questions.title: GATE CE 2017 Set 1 | CE Q50
questions.subject: Geotechnical Engineering (Soil)
questions.question: A consolidated undrained (CU) triaxial compression test is conducted on a normally consolidated clay at a confining pressure of 100 kPa. The deviator stress at failure is 80 kPa, and the pore-water pressure measured at failure is 50 kPa. The effective angle of internal friction (in degrees, up to one decimal place) of the soil is _______________
questions.explanation:
Soil Mechanics | Shear Strength

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Test type: Consolidated Undrained (CU) triaxial test
    • Soil: Normally consolidated (NC) clay
    • Confining pressure: \(\sigma_3 = 100\text{ kPa}\)
    • Deviator stress at failure: \(\sigma_d = 80\text{ kPa}\)
    • Pore-water pressure at failure: \(u = 50\text{ kPa}\)
  • Aim: Determine the effective angle of internal friction (\(\phi'\)).

3. Core Concepts:

  • Effective Stresses: \(\sigma' = \sigma - u\)
  • Principal Stresses: \(\sigma_1 = \sigma_3 + \sigma_d\)
  • Mohr-Coulomb Criterion (NC clay, \(c' = 0\)):
    \[\sin\phi' = \dfrac{\sigma_1' - \sigma_3'}{\sigma_1' + \sigma_3'} \]

4. Solution Method:

  1. Calculate total major principal stress \(\sigma_1\).
  2. Calculate effective principal stresses \(\sigma_1'\) and \(\sigma_3'\).
  3. Apply the effective stress Mohr-Coulomb criterion for \(c' = 0\) to solve for \(\phi'\).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Total principal stresses:
    \[\sigma_3 = 100\text{ kPa}, \quad \sigma_1 = 100 + 80 = 180\text{ kPa} \]
  2. Effective principal stresses:
    \[\sigma_3' = 100 - 50 = 50\text{ kPa}, \quad \sigma_1' = 180 - 50 = 130\text{ kPa} \]
  3. Calculate \(\phi'\):
    \[\sin\phi' = \dfrac{130 - 50}{130 + 50} = \dfrac{80}{180} = \dfrac{4}{9} = 0.4444 \]\[\phi' = \arcsin(0.4444) \approx 26.4^\circ \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 26.4°  |  Accepted key range: 25.5 to 27.0

questions.title: GATE CE 2017 Set 1 | CE Q51
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: An effective rainfall of 2-hour duration produced a flood hydrograph peak of 200 m³/s. The flood hydrograph has a base flow of 20 m³/s. If the spatial average rainfall in the watershed for the duration of storm is 2 cm and the average loss rate is 0.4 cm/hour, the peak of 2-hour unit hydrograph (in m³/s-cm, up to one decimal place) is _______________
questions.explanation:
Hydrology | Unit Hydrograph

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Storm duration: \(t_r = 2\text{ hours}\)
    • Flood hydrograph peak: \(200\text{ m}^3/\text{s}\)
    • Base flow: \(20\text{ m}^3/\text{s}\) (constant)
    • Total precipitation: \(P = 2\text{ cm}\)
    • Average loss rate (\(\phi\)-index): \(0.4\text{ cm/hr}\)
  • Aim: Calculate the peak of the 2-hour unit hydrograph (in m³/s-cm).

3. Core Concepts:

  • Direct Runoff Hydrograph (DRH):
    \[\text{DRH Ordinate} = \text{Flood Hydrograph Ordinate} - \text{Base Flow} \]
  • Effective Rainfall (\(R\)):
    \[R = P - \text{Total Losses} \]
  • Unit Hydrograph Proportionality:
    \[\text{Peak of UH} = \dfrac{\text{Peak of DRH}}{R} \]

4. Solution Method:

  1. Isolate the DRH peak by subtracting base flow from total flood peak.
  2. Calculate total rainfall loss over storm duration.
  3. Calculate effective rainfall depth \(R\).
  4. Divide DRH peak by \(R\) for UH peak.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Peak of DRH:
    \[Q_{p,DRH} = 200 - 20 = 180\text{ m}^3/\text{s} \]
  2. Total losses:
    \[\text{Total Loss} = 0.4\text{ cm/hr} \times 2\text{ hr} = 0.8\text{ cm} \]
  3. Effective rainfall:
    \[R = 2.0 - 0.8 = 1.2\text{ cm} \]
  4. Peak of unit hydrograph:
    \[U_p = \dfrac{180}{1.2} = 150\text{ m}^3/\text{s-cm} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 150.0 m³/s-cm  |  Accepted key range: 149.0 to 151.0

questions.title: GATE CE 2017 Set 1 | CE Q52
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question: The equivalent sound power level (in dB) of the four sources with the noise levels of 60 dB, 69 dB, 70 dB and 79 dB is _______________
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Noise Pollution

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data: Noise levels of four independent sources: \(L_1 = 60\text{ dB}\), \(L_2 = 69\text{ dB}\), \(L_3 = 70\text{ dB}\), \(L_4 = 79\text{ dB}\).
  • Aim: Determine the equivalent total sound level (\(L_{eq}\)) when all sources operate simultaneously.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Logarithmic Addition: Sound levels in dB cannot be added algebraically. The intensity ratio is: \(I/I_0 = 10^{L/10}\)
  • Equivalent Sound Level:
    \[L_{eq} = 10\log_{10}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} 10^{L_i/10}\right) \]

4. Solution Method:

  1. Convert each dB value to its acoustic intensity ratio \(10^{L/10}\).
  2. Sum the linear ratios.
  3. Convert back to dB using \(10\log_{10}\).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Intensity ratios and summation:
    \[\sum 10^{L_i/10} = 10^{6} + 10^{6.9} + 10^{7} + 10^{7.9} \]\[= 1{,}000{,}000 + 7{,}943{,}282 + 10{,}000{,}000 + 79{,}432{,}824 \]\[= 98{,}376{,}106 \]
  2. Convert back to dB:
    \[L_{eq} = 10\log_{10}(98{,}376{,}106) = 10 \times 7.9929 \approx 79.9\text{ dB} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 79.9 dB  |  Accepted key range: 79 to 81

questions.title: GATE CE 2017 Set 1 | CE Q53
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question:
The spherical grit particles, having a radius of 0.01 mm and specific gravity of 3.0, need to be separated in a settling chamber. It is given that
• g = 9.81 m/s²
• the density of the liquid in the settling chamber = 1000 kg/m³
• the kinematic viscosity of the liquid in the settling chamber = 10⁻⁶ m²/s
Assuming laminar conditions, the settling velocity (in mm/s, up to one decimal place) is _______________
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Water Treatment (Sedimentation)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Particle radius: \(r = 0.01 ext{ mm}\)
    • Specific gravity of grit: \(G_s = 3.0\)
    • \(g = 9.81 ext{ m/s}^2\), \( ho_l = 1000 ext{ kg/m}^3\)
    • Kinematic viscosity: \( u = 10^{-6} ext{ m}^2/ ext{s}\)
    • Flow regime: Laminar
  • Aim: Calculate the terminal settling velocity (\(V_s\)) in mm/s.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Stokes' Law (laminar settling, \(Re < 1\)):
    \[V_s = \dfrac{g\,(G_s - 1)\,d^2}{18\, u} \]where \(d\) is the particle diameter and \( u\) is the kinematic viscosity.

4. Solution Method:

  1. Extract diameter from given radius; convert to SI (meters).
  2. Substitute into Stokes' Law to get velocity in m/s.
  3. Convert to mm/s.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Unit preparation:
    \[d = 2 imes 0.01 ext{ mm} = 0.02 ext{ mm} = 2 imes 10^{-5} ext{ m} \]\[G_s - 1 = 2.0 \]
  2. Apply Stokes' Law:
    \[V_s = \dfrac{9.81 imes 2.0 imes (2 imes 10^{-5})^2}{18 imes 10^{-6}} = \dfrac{19.62 imes 4 imes 10^{-10}}{18 imes 10^{-6}} = \dfrac{78.48 imes 10^{-10}}{18 imes 10^{-6}} = 4.36 imes 10^{-4} ext{ m/s} \]
  3. Convert to mm/s:
    \[V_s = 4.36 imes 10^{-4} imes 1000 = 0.436 ext{ mm/s} \approx 0.4 ext{ mm/s} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 0.4 mm/s  |  Accepted key range: 0.3 to 0.5

questions.title: GATE CE 2017 Set 1 | CE Q54
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question:
Two wastewater streams A and B, having an identical ultimate BOD are getting mixed to form the stream C. The temperature of the stream A is 20°C and the temperature of the stream C is 10°C. It is given that
• the 5-day BOD of the stream A measured at 20°C = 50 mg/l
• BOD rate constant (base 10) at 20°C = 0.115 per day
• temperature coefficient = 1.135
The 5-day BOD (in mg/l, up to one decimal place) of the stream C, calculated at 10°C, is _______________
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Wastewater Characteristics (BOD)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Streams A and B have identical ultimate BOD (\(L_0\))
    • Stream A: \(T_A = 20^\circ\text{C}\), \(y_{5,20} = 50\text{ mg/l}\)
    • Base-10 BOD rate constant at 20°C: \(K_{D,20} = 0.115\text{ day}^{-1}\)
    • Temperature coefficient: \(\theta = 1.135\)
    • Stream C (mixture): \(T_C = 10^\circ\text{C}\)
  • Aim: Determine the 5-day BOD of Stream C at 10°C (\(y_{5,10}\)).

3. Core Concepts:

  • Ultimate BOD Invariance: Since streams A and B have the same \(L_0\), any mixture (Stream C) retains the same \(L_{0C} = L_0\).
  • BOD Kinetics (Base-10):
    \[y_t = L_0\left(1 - 10^{-K_D \cdot t}\right) \]
  • Temperature Correction:
    \[K_{D,T} = K_{D,20} \cdot \theta^{(T-20)} \]

4. Solution Method:

  1. Use 20°C data from Stream A to find \(L_0\).
  2. Adjust \(K_D\) to 10°C using the temperature coefficient \(\theta\).
  3. Calculate 5-day BOD of Stream C at 10°C.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Determine ultimate BOD (\(L_0\)):
    \[50 = L_0\left(1 - 10^{-0.115 \times 5}\right) = L_0\left(1 - 10^{-0.575}\right) \]\[50 = L_0(1 - 0.26607) = L_0 \times 0.73393 \]\[L_0 = \dfrac{50}{0.73393} = 68.13\text{ mg/l} \]
  2. Temperature correction for \(K_D\):
    \[K_{D,10} = 0.115 \times (1.135)^{(10-20)} = 0.115 \times (1.135)^{-10} = 0.115 \times 0.28179 = 0.03241\text{ day}^{-1} \]
  3. 5-day BOD at 10°C:
    \[y_{5,10} = 68.13 \times \left(1 - 10^{-0.03241 \times 5}\right) = 68.13 \times \left(1 - 10^{-0.16205}\right) \]\[= 68.13 \times (1 - 0.68857) = 68.13 \times 0.31143 \approx 21.2\text{ mg/l} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 21.2 mg/l  |  Accepted key range: 20.0 to 22.0

questions.title: GATE CE 2017 Set 1 | CE Q55
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question: The wastewater having an organic concentration of 54 mg/l is flowing at a steady rate of 0.8 m³/day through a detention tank of dimensions 2 m × 4 m × 2 m. If the contents of the tank are well mixed and the decay constant is 0.1 per day, the outlet concentration (in mg/l, up to one decimal place) is _______________
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Reactor Kinetics

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Inlet concentration: \(C_{in} = 54\text{ mg/l}\)
    • Flow rate: \(Q = 0.8\text{ m}^3/\text{day}\)
    • Tank dimensions: \(2\text{ m} \times 4\text{ m} \times 2\text{ m}\) (well-mixed)
    • First-order decay constant: \(k = 0.1\text{ day}^{-1}\)
  • Aim: Calculate the steady-state outlet concentration (\(C_{out}\)).

3. Core Concepts:

  • Reactor Type: "Well-mixed" implies a Completely Mixed Flow Reactor (CMFR / CSTR).
  • Hydraulic Retention Time: \(\theta = V/Q\)
  • Steady-State Mass Balance (first-order decay, accumulation \(= 0\)):
    \[Q\,C_{in} - Q\,C_{out} - V k\,C_{out} = 0 \implies C_{out} = \dfrac{C_{in}}{1 + k\theta} \]

4. Solution Method:

  1. Calculate tank volume \(V\).
  2. Determine HRT \(\theta = V/Q\).
  3. Apply the CMFR steady-state equation to find \(C_{out}\).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Tank volume and HRT:
    \[V = 2 \times 4 \times 2 = 16\text{ m}^3 \]\[\theta = \dfrac{16}{0.8} = 20\text{ days} \]
  2. Effluent concentration:
    \[C_{out} = \dfrac{54}{1 + (0.1 \times 20)} = \dfrac{54}{1 + 2} = \dfrac{54}{3} = 18.0\text{ mg/l} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 18.0 mg/l  |  Accepted key range: 17.9 to 18.1

questions.title: GATE CE 2017 Set 1 | GA Q56
questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.question: The bacteria in milk are destroyed when it _______________ heated to 80 degree Celsius.
questions.explanation:
Verbal Aptitude → Basic English Grammar

Problem Analysis

  • Taxonomy: Recall / Comprehension
  • Given: A sentence detailing a scientific fact about bacteria in milk being destroyed at 80 degrees Celsius.
  • Find: The correct verb tense to complete the sentence from the options: "would be", "will be", "is", and "was".
  • Concepts used: Subject-verb agreement and proper tense usage for universal truths.

Solution

  • In English grammar, universal truths, general scientific facts, and habitual actions are always expressed in the simple present tense.
  • The sentence describes a standard, repeatable physical process (destroying bacteria via heating).
  • Therefore, the simple present tense "is" must be used to maintain grammatical correctness and factual consistency.

Final Answer

Answer: is
Correct option: (C)

questions.title: GATE CE 2017 Set 1 | GA Q57
questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.question: _______________ with someone else’s email account is now a very serious offence.
questions.explanation:
Verbal Aptitude → Vocabulary

Problem Analysis

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension / Application
  • Given: A sentence stating that interfering with someone else's email account is a serious offence.
  • Find: The most appropriate word to fill in the blank from the options: "Involving", "Assisting", "Tampering", "Incubating".
  • Concepts used: Contextual vocabulary and word meaning.

Solution

The context of the sentence implies an unauthorized, malicious, or illegal interaction with an email account. Evaluating each option:

  • Involving / Assisting: Generally have positive or neutral connotations and do not fit the preposition "with" seamlessly in the context of committing an offence.
  • Incubating: A biological or developmental term — entirely irrelevant here.
  • Tampering: Means to interfere with something in order to cause damage or make unauthorized alterations. This aligns perfectly with the legal/security context of the sentence.

Final Answer

Answer: Tampering
Correct option: (C)

questions.title: GATE CE 2017 Set 1 | GA Q58
questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.question:
Consider the following sentences:
All benches are beds. No bed is a bulb. Some bulbs are lamps.
Which of the following can be inferred?
i. Some beds are lamps.
ii. Some lamps are beds.
questions.explanation:
Analytical Aptitude → Logic

Problem Analysis

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given: Three premises:
    1. All benches are beds.
    2. No bed is a bulb.
    3. Some bulbs are lamps.
  • Find: Whether conclusion (i) "Some beds are lamps" and/or (ii) "Some lamps are beds" can be inferred.
  • Concepts used: Syllogism (Deductive reasoning).

Solution

Analyze the premises step-by-step:

  1. All benches are beds. (Universal Affirmative)
  2. No bed is a bulb. (Universal Negative) \(\Rightarrow\) By conversion: No bulb is a bed.
  3. Some bulbs are lamps. (Particular Affirmative) \(\Rightarrow\) By conversion: Some lamps are bulbs.

Deduce the relationship between beds and lamps:

  • Combining premises 2 and 3: if No bed is a bulb and Some bulbs are lamps, the specific lamps which are bulbs can never be beds.
  • The valid deduction is: Some lamps are not beds.

Check the given inferences:

  • (i) Some beds are lamps: Invalid — no positive relationship is established between beds and lamps.
  • (ii) Some lamps are beds: Invalid — we can only deduce that some lamps are not beds; we cannot claim any are.

Both conclusions fail to logically follow.

Final Answer

Answer: Neither (i) nor (ii)
Correct option: (D)

questions.question: If the radius of a right circular cone is increased by 50%, its volume increases by
questions.explanation:

Problem Analysis

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given: The radius of a right circular cone is increased by 50%.
  • Find: The percentage increase in its volume.
  • Concepts used: Volume of a cone, percentage change.

Solution

The volume of a right circular cone is given by:

\[V = \dfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h\]

Since only the radius is changing, assume the height \(h\) remains constant. Let the initial radius be \(r\). The new radius after a 50% increase:

\[r_{new} = r + 0.5r = 1.5r\]

Calculate the new volume:

\[V_{new} = \dfrac{1}{3}\pi (1.5r)^2 h = \dfrac{1}{3}\pi (2.25r^2) h = 2.25 \cdot V_{initial}\]

Calculate the percentage increase:

\[\text{Increase} = \dfrac{V_{new} - V_{initial}}{V_{initial}} \times 100\% = \dfrac{2.25V - V}{V} \times 100\% = 1.25 \times 100\% = 125\%\]

Final Answer

Answer: 125%
Correct option: (C)

questions.question: The following sequence of numbers is arranged in increasing order: 1, x, x, x, y, y, 9, 16, 18. Given that the mean and median are equal, and are also equal to twice the mode, the value of y is
questions.explanation:
Quantitative Aptitude → Elementary Statistics and Probability

Problem Analysis

  • Taxonomy: Application / Analysis
  • Given: An ordered sequence of 9 numbers: \(1, x, x, x, y, y, 9, 16, 18\). A condition stating that the mean and median are equal, and both equal twice the mode.
  • Find: The value of \(y\).
  • Concepts used: Mean, Median, Mode definitions and algebraic formulation.

Solution

Step 1: Identify the Mode. The number \(x\) appears three times and \(y\) appears twice. The highest frequency belongs to \(x\):

\[\text{Mode} = x\]

Step 2: Identify the Median. In an ordered list of 9 numbers, the median is the 5th term:

\[\text{Median} = y\]

Step 3: Formulate the Mean.

\[\text{Sum} = 1 + 3x + 2y + 9 + 16 + 18 = 3x + 2y + 44\]\[\text{Mean} = \dfrac{3x + 2y + 44}{9}\]

Step 4: Apply the given conditions. We are given \(\text{Mean} = \text{Median} = 2 \times \text{Mode}\).

  • From \(\text{Median} = 2 \times \text{Mode}\): \(y = 2x \Rightarrow x = 0.5y\)
  • From \(\text{Mean} = \text{Median}\): \(\dfrac{3x + 2y + 44}{9} = y\)

Step 5: Solve. Substitute \(x = 0.5y\):

\[3(0.5y) + 2y + 44 = 9y\]\[1.5y + 2y + 44 = 9y\]\[3.5y + 44 = 9y\]\[5.5y = 44 \implies y = \dfrac{44}{5.5} = 8\]

Final Answer

Answer: \(y = 8\)
Correct option: (D)

  • Taxonomy: Analysis / Application
  • Given: Rules for hostel allocation based strictly on seniority. Students can move if a preferred room is available. Lower-ranked students are bumped if a higher-ranked student wants their room.
    Current allocations: Amar in P, Anthony in Q, Ajit in S.
    Preferences: Amar (R, S, Q), Akbar (R, S), Anthony (P), Ajit (Q, P, R).

  • Concepts used: Sequential logic, priority-based assignment.

Solution

Process the students strictly in order of seniority (Rank 1 to 4):

  • Rank 1 — Amar (currently in P, wants R, S, Q): R is empty → Amar moves to R.
    State: Amar in R, Anthony in Q, Ajit in S, P is empty.
  • Rank 2 — Akbar (no room, wants R, S): R is taken by Amar (Rank 1) — cannot bump. S is taken by Ajit (Rank 4) — Akbar outranks Ajit, so Akbar bumps Ajit and takes S.

questions.question: The last digit of \((2171)^7 + (2172)^9 + (2173)^{11} + (2174)^{13}\) is
questions.explanation:
Quantitative Aptitude → Numerical Computation and Estimation

Problem Analysis

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given: The expression \((2171)^7 + (2172)^9 + (2173)^{11} + (2174)^{13}\).
  • Find: The last digit (unit digit) of the evaluated sum.
  • Concepts used: Number theory, cyclicity of unit digits.

Solution

The unit digit of an exponentiated number depends only on the unit digit of its base. Evaluate each term using cyclicity rules:

  • Term 1: \((2171)^7 \rightarrow 1^7\) — Any power of 1 ends in 1. Unit digit = 1.
  • Term 2: \((2172)^9 \rightarrow 2^9\) — Cyclicity of 2 is 4 (pattern: 2, 4, 8, 6). \(9 \div 4\) leaves remainder 1, so unit digit matches \(2^1 = 2\). Unit digit = 2.
  • Term 3: \((2173)^{11} \rightarrow 3^{11}\) — Cyclicity of 3 is 4 (pattern: 3, 9, 7, 1). \(11 \div 4\) leaves remainder 3, so unit digit matches \(3^3 = 27 \rightarrow 7\). Unit digit = 7.
  • Term 4: \((2174)^{13} \rightarrow 4^{13}\) — Cyclicity of 4 is 2 (odd power → 4, even power → 6). 13 is odd. Unit digit = 4.

Sum the unit digits:

\[1 + 2 + 7 + 4 = 14\]

The unit digit of 14 is 4.

Final Answer

Answer: 4
Correct option: (B)

questions.question: Two machines M1 and M2 are able to execute any of four jobs P, Q, R and S. The machines can perform one job on one object at a time. Jobs P, Q, R and S take 30 minutes, 20 minutes, 60 minutes and 15 minutes each respectively. There are 10 objects each requiring exactly 1 job. Job P is to be performed on 2 objects. Job Q on 3 objects. Job R on 1 object and Job S on 4 objects. What is the minimum time needed to complete all the jobs?
questions.explanation:
Quantitative Aptitude → Numerical Computation and Estimation

Problem Analysis

  • Taxonomy: Analysis / Synthesis
  • Given: Two machines (M1, M2) can perform jobs P, Q, R, S.
    Durations: P = 30 min, Q = 20 min, R = 60 min, S = 15 min.
    Quantities: 2 of P, 3 of Q, 1 of R, 4 of S.
  • Find: The absolute minimum time required to complete all jobs.
  • Concepts used: Resource scheduling, optimization.

Solution

Step 1: Calculate total workload.

  • Job P: \(2 \times 30 = 60\) min
  • Job Q: \(3 \times 20 = 60\) min
  • Job R: \(1 \times 60 = 60\) min
  • Job S: \(4 \times 15 = 60\) min
  • Total Work = \(60 + 60 + 60 + 60 = 240\) minutes.

Step 2: Determine theoretical minimum. With 2 identical parallel machines:

\[\text{Minimum Time} = \dfrac{\text{Total Work}}{2} = \dfrac{240}{2} = 120 \text{ minutes} = 2 \text{ hours}\]

Step 3: Validate with an optimal schedule.

  • M1: 1 Job R (60 min) + 2 Jobs P (\(2 \times 30\) min) = 120 min.
  • M2: 3 Jobs Q (\(3 \times 20\) min) + 4 Jobs S (\(4 \times 15\) min) = 120 min.

Both machines are fully utilized for exactly 120 minutes without conflict, confirming the optimal schedule is achievable.

Final Answer

Answer: 2 hours
Correct option: (A)
